HEADLINE: Goldman arrives in GE race
INTRO: Goldman Sachs Special Situations Group has emerged as one of Lonestar Capital Management's financing partners in the race for GE Capital's commercial assets.
TEXT:
Goldman Sachs Special Situations Group has emerged as one of Lonestar Capital Management's financing partners in the race for GE Capital's commercial assets.

Street Talk also understands that GE and adviser Morgan Stanley have pushed back the final bid date after the auction was due to wrap up next week.

This column revealed Lonestar had drafted in investment bank Citi as an adviser, in addition to Houlihan Lokey.

The portfolio has exposure to five different asset pools including debtor finance, aviation finance and asset-backed lending. GE's auction is part of a global divestment drive by the conglomerate as it seeks to streamline its businesses and pull back from capital intensive finance divisions.

China's HNA Group and Sankaty Partners are also still in the running for the Australian assets.

Meanwhile, HNA is said to have stepped up its efforts in ANZ Banking Group's Esanda Dealer Finance auction.

The Chinese conglomerate is up against Macquarie Group and Pepper Group in the Esanda sale.

Newly listed non-bank lender Pepper has assembled a consortium of equity partners, senior lenders and mezzanine lenders.

HEADLINE: Link IPO priced amid volatility; cornerstone investor secured
INTRO: Link Group's initial public offering is set to be priced at 21 to 24-times forecast 2016 financial year profit, valuing its equity at $2 billion to $2.3 billion, as revealed by Street Talk Online on Tuesday.
TEXT:
Link Group's initial public offering is set to be priced at 21 to 24-times forecast 2016 financial year profit, valuing its equity at $2 billion to $2.3 billion, as revealed by Street Talk Online on Tuesday.

Link's enterprise value has been pegged at between $2.3 billion and $2.6 billion while the EV/EBITDA range is 13 times to 15 times.

Link will lodge its prospectus on Wednesday morning, pushing ahead with the $900 million-odd equity offer despite volatility in the wider equity market following a pre-deal roadshow by sponsor brokers Citi, Deutsche Bank, Macquarie Capital and UBS.

Early indications from key investors are understood to have been positive.

The prospectus is expected to confirm Link is seeking to raise about $900 million, while existing investors, including Pacific Equity Partners, will collectively sell less than 25 per cent of their pre-IPO stake.

The offer has been priced in line with analyst valuations, released by the joint lead managers.

The analysts valued the company at $2.3 billion to $3.2 billion on an enterprise value basis, which implied 12.7-times to 17.7-times earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation.

It is also understood the IPO may have attracted a cornerstone investor for $100 million through the offer range.

Investor sources said the backer could be a client of the group, reflecting recent trends towards direct investment from key pension fund managers.

Management is understood to have met with pension funds earlier in the year.

Cornerstone backing, from a Link client, would be likely to provide other shareholders with further comfort.

Link is slated to list on October 27.

HEADLINE: Arrium board meets on Moly-Cop auction
INTRO: Arrium has received indicative bids for its Moly-Cop grinding media business from global private equity firms Blackstone Group and TPG.
TEXT:
Arrium has received indicative bids for its Moly-Cop grinding media business from global private equity firms Blackstone Group and TPG.

It's understood Arrium held a board meeting on Monday to talk about the sale and the embattled mining and steel company will make a decision this week as to whether it moves forward with the process after the indicative round.

Sources said the sale was under pressure and there were fewer than five bids in total, including Blackstone, TPG (which is running its approach out of the US) and a trade buyer. However, those in the Arrium camp say there were more than 10 indicative offers lodged.

Should the company move forward with the sale its advisers, UBS and Lazard, will kick off a round of site visits and management presentations.

Moly-Cop's operations span Australia, Latin America, North America and Indonesia, so it could be months before the second bidding round and final close may not come until the new year.

The sale would be further de-stabilised should Arrium's lenders get nervous and start selling their exposure to its $1.7 billion debt pile.

Street Talk revealed two of Arrium's big four Australian banks in June had approached distressed debt funds about selling their exposure to the company.

Arrium had targeted a lofty $2 billion price target for Moly-Cop. The company has forecast Moly-Cop's earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation to hit $US190 million ($265 million) in fiscal 2016.

Some banks reckon acquisition financing of around 5 times earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation would be possible, while others suggest this is too aggressive in a weak commodity price environment.

Elsewhere, Dongfang Modern will close its initial public offering on Thursday, after exceeding its $39 million minimum subscription target.

The Chinese tangerine and navel orange grower is expected to be valued around $400 million and generate earnings in excess of $75 million.

HEADLINE: APA Group bid for Iona Gas Plant runs into ACCC trouble
INTRO: APA Group's bid for EnergyAustralia's Iona Gas Plant is in serious doubt, with the competition watchdog set to make it almost impossible for APA to buy Iona under the existing auction timetable.
TEXT:
APA Group's bid for EnergyAustralia's Iona Gas Plant is in serious doubt, with the competition watchdog set to make it almost impossible for APA to buy Iona under the existing auction timetable.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission is expected to announce on Wednesday that it needs more time to investigate APA's bid for Iona, as revealed by Street Talk Online, and plans to release a statement of issues in coming days.

APA is likely to need another two months to address the issues, while binding offers for Iona are also believed to be due on Wednesday.

APA is widely viewed as Iona's most logical buyer. The $10 billion listed pipeline owner owns and operates the SEA Gas Pipeline, which transports gas from Iona into the South Australian market, and the South West Pipeline, which takes gas into Victoria.

However, it seems unlikely APA would be willing to submit a binding bid while the competition watchdog's investigation was ongoing.

It means the auction, under its existing structure, is in favour of rival bidders, which include QIC Ltd and REST Industry Super, who will no doubt reconsider their position following APA's position.

Of course EnergyAustralia, and adviser Lazard, could always alter the timetable to make way for the ACCC's delay. However it would be extremely late in the process to make any drastic changes.

APA Group chief executive Mick McCormack has publicly expressed his frustration with the ACCC as recently as last month, telling shareholders: "I can't get out of bed without the ACCC sending something to me".

"As to any substance in their inquiries [at Iona], I'm sure they'll come back with a blank sheet," he said, when addressing analysts and investors on a results call in August.

The ACCC and the acquisitive APA have a long history. The ACCC claimed a small win in 2012 though, when APA agreed to sell the Moomba to Adelaide Pipeline System as part of its $1.8 billion acquisition of Hastings Diversified Utilities Fund. However APA is yet to have an acquisition blocked.

The Iona facility, built and opened by EnergyAustralia in 2008, is used to store gas and helps retailers including EnergyAustralia, AGL Energy and Origin Energy, and second-tier players Red Energy and Simply Energy manage supply in peak and off-peak periods.

Iona has $80 million annual earnings and is expected to fetch 13 to 20-times earnings at auction, in line with other recent infrastructure transactions.

Street Talk revealed EnergyAustralia was considering selling the asset in June and appointed Lazard to test buyer interest. The sale was triggered after the utilities company received inbound approaches for the asset.

HEADLINE: Wylie tweaks Tanarra portfolio with Geotech sale
INTRO: Geotech Group is on track to be Tanarra Capital's first divestment since investment banking veteran John Wylie took over the management rights of the old Lazard Private Equity.
TEXT:
Geotech Group is on track to be Tanarra Capital's first divestment since investment banking veteran John Wylie took over the management rights of the old Lazard Private Equity.

As revealed by Street Talk Online, Tanarra has launched the Geotech sale and sent out flyers to prospective buyers.

The civil engineering and contracting group, which owns the No.2 rail construction business in Australia, Coleman Rail, is forecast to generate $220 million in revenue in financial year 2015, on earnings before interest and tax of $25 million, according to the sale flyer obtained by Street Talk.

The most logical acquirer is Downer EDI, although it is understood multiple private equity and trade buyers have expressed interest.

Street Talk revealed in May that Wylie was in negotiations to take over the management rights to Lazard's private equity fund in Australia. He subsequently rebadged the firm Tanarra and is now shaping the investment portfolio.

Tanarra also holds an 18 per cent stake in compression tights and triathlon suits 2XU, which has been earmarked for sale via an initial public offering.

Geotech's board is chaired by Dieter Adamsas, a former deputy chief executive officer and CFO of Leighton Holdings.

The Melbourne-based company "is and has been in recent years, prime contractor on some of Australia's most significant infrastructure projects, especially in rail, including the $5 billion Victorian regional rail project and the $300 million Adelaide metro rail network project," according to the flyer. Its key markets "enjoy highly attractive growth prospects over the next decade" while "a consistent base load of recurring work delivers strong gross profit margin of circa 20 per cent year on year."

State and federal governments are planning to spend more than $80 billion on infrastructure over the next 10 years.

The flyer said Geotech was well positioned to take advantage of this investment pipeline, particularly the rail and specialist engineering projects, but it would be able to win more projects with the backing of a global industry player's balance sheet and resources.

The company is most dominant in Victoria but also has projects in Queensland, NSW, Western Australia and South Australia.

HEADLINE: Business backs Turnbull's new reform push
INTRO: Company directors have backed Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull's decision to seek consensus on reform priorities, with business, community and union leaders saying his approach was creating "a strong sense of optimism".
TEXT:
Company directors have backed Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull's decision to seek consensus on reform priorities, with business, community and union leaders saying his approach was creating "a strong sense of optimism".

"I think it's so palpable you can feel it. There's a much more engaging discussion taking place. I think it's in the broader community as well as the business community," said KPMG Australia chairman Peter Nash.

"I think Turnbull has struck a chord because Australians at large like their politicians close to the centre."

Mr Nash said it was to the credit of The Australian Financial Review and The Australian newspapers that they had created an environment for debate and captured the attention of the new Prime Minister by holding reform summits.

"I think that Turnbull coming in has provided the opportunity for a fresh look with no strings attached at the dialogue that took place," he said.

"I think that under the previous regime both from a Labor and Liberal perspective it was sort of, 'Can we forget about that and move on?'."

Mr Nash said it was promising that Mr Turnbull was consulting his colleagues and not making policy on the run.

But the Prime Minister would eventually have to "walk the walk" and while business hoped this would result in progressive policy, "that's the piece that's still to take place at the moment".

Tony Shepherd, chairman of Macquarie Specialised Asset Management and former chairman of WestConnex and Transfield Services, said Mr Turnbull's agreement to meet the leading business, civil society and union leaders was "a great move" and a "very positive development".

"Getting in a new Prime Minister does enable you to refresh things and go back over what you have considered before. So I think it's a great opportunity to reset."

Mr Shepherd praised the Business Council of Australia - he is a former president - for pushing the reform agenda forward over the years and said it was good that it had "prime ministerial endorsement".

Innes Willox, chief executive of the Australian Industry Group, said Mr Turnbull's embrace of the reform summits was a chance to "reframe the economy for the 21st century".

"We need agreements that our economy is low and slow when it comes to growth, that we have enormous competitive challenges, we have emerging trends around the sharing economy, Uber, Airbnb and the like, automation, our workplaces are changing, [and] our expectations of our workforce are changing," Mr Willox said.

Mr Nash said the most exciting thing about Mr Turnbull was his understanding of innovation, the new economy and disruption - which would be the source of future jobs.

"You really get the sense that he understands the importance they they pose for the economy, whereas it was entirely unclear where the previous group stood on this," he said.

"Having someone who understands this is a massive step forward. I think we ran the risk of falling behind in terms of international competitiveness. It's still a risk but now we seem to be having the right discussion and having the right issues on the table."

HEADLINE: Why Bolt's wrong about Abbott and Turnbull
INTRO: Having watching the vanquished of Australian politics squeal like stuck pigs over this past fortnight, it's hard not to draw the obvious conclusion that "I will go quietly" means precisely the opposite.
TEXT:
Having watching the vanquished of Australian politics squeal like stuck pigs over this past fortnight, it's hard not to draw the obvious conclusion that "I will go quietly" means precisely the opposite.

Before the taste of defeat had evaporated from his morning croissant, Tony Abbott himself promised there'd be "no wrecking, no undermining, and no sniping" from him, right before he engaged in only that: the accidental wetsuit collision with the Daily Telegraph reporter ("Scott Morrison is a liar"); confession with Ray Hadley ("Seriously, I would've won") and the most damning of all, the interview with his blood brother Simon Benson ("Malcolm is actually me in disguise").

Then Maurice Newman gets the sack as Abbott's Prime Ministerial business adviser. Why? According to him: "There was little chance I would have survived under Turnbull because I am not his type of businessman… I believe in smaller government. I believe in markets." Funny, from a bloke who advised a PM whose idea of smaller government consisted of chaplains in schools and (until he could defend it no longer) taxpayers replacing the private sector salaries of new mothers. As for this belief in markets, what about squibbing tax reform (except to raise them), industrial relations reform, blocking a major agri-takeover by a US company and winking at $35 billion of submarines without a real tender, just a nod to Japan (the extremely tentative neighbour to our biggest economic partner)?

Then that turkey Andrew Bolt. For reasons Abbott should be compared to a summer's day, he says "I won't go through the whole list", before going through the whole list.

We won't.

"See, I don't think Abbott is a great man because he's my friend. He's my friend because he's a great man."

The humility makes the eyes water. How lucky you are if Bolt picks you out of a crowd. And the now-hackneyed chiasmus, the "flipper" of writing, still such a lovely literary device until JFK ruined it. Even a Herald Sun blogger can flip a sentence these days. Someone must translate his musings into Latin and rocket them to Mars before the conflagration comes and it's too late!

But Bolt's shopping list of Abbott injustice is actually right. He wasn't a failure because he was "a woman hater" or a "crash-through insensitive bully with no people skills" or "too loyal" or "a homophobe". The real reason was because he listened to people like you, Andrew. And Maurice Newman and Piers Akerman and Miranda Devine, and then wondered why middle Australia could only conclude that he was the weirdo they always suspected he was. That's why Abbott failed, and you don't have to be a leftie - not even a little bit - to think so.

HEADLINE: Lessons for all in Glencore collapse
INTRO: Before you jump on the Glencore bankruptcy bandwagon consider these perspectives from an investment banker, a debt market investor, an equity trading desk veteran, a credit rating analyst, a hedge fund manager and, believe it or not, the company itself.
TEXT:
Before you jump on the Glencore bankruptcy bandwagon consider these perspectives from an investment banker, a debt market investor, an equity trading desk veteran, a credit rating analyst, a hedge fund manager and, believe it or not, the company itself.

But first, here is the controversial view of the world's biggest commodities trader from the analyst at Investec Bank who triggered a 30 per cent plunge in the company's share price on Monday.

Investec's Hunter Hillcoat said in a note to clients: "At current spot prices, all else being the same, Glencore's equity value is zero", according to The Financial Times.

He went on to say that "using a PE-based approach to evaluate equity value going forward, in proportion to debt, we note that the heavily indebted companies could see almost all equity value eliminated under spot conditions, leaving nothing for shareholders", according to Zerohedge.

In other words, the total equity on the Glencore balance sheet of $US47.45 billion is worthless.

While that is a scary conclusion for Glencore shareholders to digest, it was Hillcoat's statements in relation to Glencore's readily marketable inventories or RMI, which really put the cat amongst the pigeons.

RMI is the physical commodities trading inventory owned by Glencore and used in its day-to-day business of trading commodities on global exchanges and over the counter. The RMI is worth about $US18 billion.

Hillcoat gives Glencore no credit for something which the company and credit ratings agencies regard as being as good as cash.

In other words, he is saying that the debt burden at Glencore is not the net amount of $US28 billion the company has repeatedly referred to in market announcements and in meetings with investors.

Instead, it is $US45 billion. That puts a very different complexion on a company with a market capitalisation of about $US16.7 billion.

It is against that confusing backdrop that Chanticleer sought the views of various market players.

The investment banker, who did not want to be named, said the collapse in Glencore's share price marked a turning point in the market's tolerance of debt in the resources sector.

He argues that investors are not only sending a message to Glencore chief executive Ivan Glasenberg about the need for a less leveraged balance sheet, they are also sending a message to BHP Billiton and Rio Tinto about their unsustainable dividend policies.

The banker says BHP's Andrew Mackenzie and Rio's Sam Walsh should take on board what the markets are saying.

They should abandon capital management policies that will ultimately force them to borrow to pay dividends. He says they should return to the traditional resources industry strategy of investing for growth at the bottom of the commodities cycle.

It is noteworthy that the banker has been around long enough to have had several clashes with Glasenberg. However, they always departed as friends.

He says it would be a mistake to underestimate Glasenberg's ability to handle a crisis. Nor should investors forget the fact that he got through the global financial crisis with his business intact.

The equity trading desk veteran says that Glencore is basically a cyclical company with too much debt. "When commodity prices fall the value of the whole enterprise is clearly worth a lot less," he says.

"The value of the whole company is the enterprise value. The issue is that when you have a lot of debt, the value of the debt doesn't change. So effectively the equity piece takes a disproportionate hit. The more the debt, the greater the impact on equity."

He says Glencore is in a difficult situation because it is trying to sell assets into a sceptical market. Also, it is being seen as a proxy for betting against China.

The debt market investor, Jonathan Rochford at Narrow Road Capital, says Glencore's debt is being priced for junk status even though it has an investment-grade credit rating.

"In the risks section of the recent company presentation a fall in the copper price is listed as the biggest commodity exposure, with a 10 per cent drop reducing profit by $US615 million per half year," he says. "With copper hitting fresh lows and down around 17 per cent since June 30, there's $US2 billion dollars of earnings per annum gone. All things being equal, that has the business struggling to pay interest let alone generate a profit regardless of how much of the profit adjustments you accept. No profit means that lenders won't want to rollover debt when it matures and there's also limited ability to amortise debt from cash flows."

"Whilst the investment grade ratings (BBB/Baa2) remain for the time being the movements in the debt prices are indicating they won't last much longer," Rochford says.

"Goldman Sachs raised the possibility of downgrades last week, noting that the proposed steps to reduce debt by $US10 billion were inadequate."

The hedge fund manager is Glencore shareholder John Burbank from Passport Capital, who is on the record as shorting Glencore shares.

He said in a recent interview with RealVisionTV that energy commodities are about to be "liquidated".

He said "we are on the precipice of a liquidation in emerging markets like the fourth quarter of 1997."

However, that bearishness is not being reflected in the latest missive from Simon Redmond, the primary credit analyst at Standard & Poor's responsible for analysing Glencore.

In a note issued soon after Glencore announced a $US2.5 billion capital raising and a $IUS10 billion debt reduction plan, Redmond wrote that under the S&P base case Glencore will have adjusted EBITDA of $US9 billion to $US10 billion in 2015, proportionately consolidating three sizeable joint ventures, before a moderate increase in 2016. Importantly, Redmond gives Glencore cash credit for 90 to 75 per cent of its RMI. He includes positive commentary about the company's mining operations and its commodities trading business. "The company's very well-diversified mining operations and large-scale, long-lived, low-cost assets partly offset the cyclicality of the mining industry. The group compares well with most peers in terms of commodity diversification," he said. "We factor in our assessment that the group's cost position will further improve because of currency changes, efficiency measures, and as new projects reach full capacity. The business risk profile is further supported by Glencore's strong business position, notably thanks to the scale and scope of its marketing operations--which span from metals, oil, and coal to agricultural commodities--as well as to perceived supportive risk management and risk position."

The company itself made it clear to Chanticleer that it will bunker down and tough it out. It will go ahead with the sale of about 30 per cent of its agricultural business which is worth about $US12 billion in total.

HEADLINE: Credit bears look back to 2008 crisis
INTRO: With one more session remaining, the Australian sharemarket is poised to deliver its worst quarter in four years.
TEXT:
With one more session remaining, the Australian sharemarket is poised to deliver its worst quarter in four years.

Indeed, investors haven't endured this sort of sell-off since the major S&P ASX 200 Index fell 18 per cent in the six months ended September 2011.

Another 100 points of selling and the local sharemarket will be in bear market territory.

Amid all the fear and loathing on Tuesday, the real concern is that another sustained downturn can't be ruled out. Signs the credit markets are getting fussy and pushing up the cost of borrowing has an eerie 2007 and 2008 feel to it and backs up the theory that over the past few years the wrong sort of companies, and countries, got access to all the cheap capital.

While traders might debate the extent of any further declines, sharemarkets are set for a period of volatility as credit markets ponder the possibility of a global recession.

So far this quarter, the index is down 9.9 per cent and that follows a fall of 7.3 per cent in the three months ended June. Shares fell 13 per cent in the third quarter of 2011.

On Wall Street, the S&P 500 has also fallen into correction territory now that it has closed below 1900 for the first time since May 2014.
